etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English none, noon, non (“not one”), from Old English nān (“not one, not any, none”), from Proto-West Germanic *nain, from Proto-Germanic *nainaz (“none, nought, nothing”), equivalent to ne (“not”) +‎ one. (Regarding the different phonological development of only and one, see the note in one.)

Cognate with Scots nane (“none”), Saterland Frisian naan, neen (“no, not any, none”), West Frisian neen & gjin (“no, none”), Dutch neen & geen (“no, none”), Low German nēn, neen (“none, no one”), German nein & kein (“no, none”), Latin nōn (“not”).

quote.citation: 2006, Clive James, North Face of Soho, page 253:
quote.text: Alas, none of these people were writing the reviews.

definitions.definition: Not any of a given number or group.
(archaic outside Scotland, West Country) Not any; no (usually used only before a vowel or h):

quote.citation: 1526, [William Tyndale, transl.], The Newe Testamẽt […] (Tyndale Bible), [Worms, Germany: Peter Schöffer], →OCLC, Matthew:
quote.text: the foles toke their lampes, but toke none oyle with them.

quote.citation: 2008, James Kelman, Kieron Smith, Boy, Penguin, published 2009, page 138:
quote.text: None lasses were in the dunces' row. If one had been there people would have looked at her and felt sorry but not boys.

definitions.definition: To no extent, in no way. [from 11th c.]

quote.text: my lack of education hasn't hurt me none

definitions.definition: Not at all, not very. [from 13th c.]

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From the first sense, since they respond “none” when asked about their religion; also a play on words on nun.

definitions.definition: (chiefly American) A person without religious affiliation.

quote.citation: 2003, Jacob A. Belzen, Antoon Geels, Mysticism: A Variety of Psychological Perspectives‎[1], page 50:
quote.text: Both the religiously dis-identified ("nones") and the religiously committed report mystical experiences.

quote.citation: 2010, Robert D. Putnam, David E Campbell, American Grace: How Religion Divides and Unites Us‎[2], page 591:
quote.text: Stable nones, that is, people who report in both years that they have no religious affiliation, are, in fact, much less religious

quote.citation: 2013, Michael Corbett, Politics and Religion in the United States:
quote.text: we have grouped people into nones (no religion), Jews, Catholics, mainline Protestants, and evangelical protestants.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From French none, from Latin nōna (“ninth; ninth hour”).

definitions.definition: Alternative form of nones: the ninth hour after dawn; (Christianity) the religious service appointed to this hour.
(obsolete) Synonym of midafternoon: the time around or following noon or nones.

quote.text: None of the day, is the third quarter of the day beginning at Noon and lasting till the Sun be gone half way towards setting.

quote.citation: 1706, L.E. Dupin, “v, 43”, in D. Cotes, transl., A New Ecclesiastical History of the 16th Century, volume II:
quote.text: The last, which began at the middle of the Afternoon, i.e. at half the Time between Noon and Sun-setting, was called None, because it began at the Ninth Hour.
